text: Socrates builds his city out of need rather than from an idea. “None of us is self-sufficient,” and the first citizens, for that reason, are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, each assigned to the one work his nature fits (Republic 369b–370c). Such a small city would have no need of soldiers. Glaucon refuses it. He wants couches, side dishes, and the other furnishings of luxury, so Socrates grants him the “feverish” city (372d–373a). The growth of appetite leads at once to war: the land that fed the healthy city cannot feed the feverish one, and the city must take some of its neighbors’ land and defend its own (373d–e). A class of warriors follows of necessity. From this point, the rest of the reading is occupied by the question of the person who can be trusted with weapons. Socrates finds his model in the well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers (375a–376b). The dog gives him the first of the city’s many surprises. Since the guardian distinguishes friend from enemy by knowledge, he is already a philosopher of a kind (376b–c).
